title: No water, no moon
hookLine: the nun Chiyono's bucket bottom breaks, the moon's reflection vanishes, and she awakens

cards: An old wooden bucket, its staves held together by a hoop of bamboo. A nun carries it out at night to fetch water.
As she walks back she glances down: the full moon is floating in the water, bright and round, held right there in her bucket. Then the bamboo hoop snaps.
The staves spring apart, the bottom drops out, and the water rushes onto the ground. The moon in the bucket is gone. Tradition says that in that moment, the nun Chiyono woke up.

teach.b: Chiyono comes to us through Zen stories as a woman who practiced for a long time, working and sitting at a temple, without the breakthrough she hoped for.
Tellings differ about her life before; they agree about the bucket.
First, the moon in the water. Buddhist writing uses this picture for things that look solid and aren't. The moon in a bucket looks real; you could almost scoop it out.
But it's a reflection, lasting only as long as the water stays still and the bucket holds.

Second, the bottom falls out. Tradition gives Chiyono a short verse about that night. In plain English it says, roughly: I tried this way and that to keep the old bucket together, until the bottom fell out.
Where no water stays, no moon lives. Read that way, her years of effort were the bamboo hoop, holding things together: the bucket, the practice, the picture of what awakening should look like.
When the hoop gave way, what she'd held so carefully turned out not to be what she was looking for. Third, what's not lost. The story never says the moon left the sky.

Only the copy went, with the water. Some readers hear the self in that bucket, a reflection carried carefully from place to place. Others hear every idea of awakening, which has to spill before awakening can happen.
The story leaves room for both, and the real moon stays where it always was.

how: Chiyono's story and her verse about the broken bucket are retold in Zen collections, alongside other stories of awakening that come in an ordinary moment.

games.q: no water, no moon: tap the pairs.
p: a nun who woke up as it spilled

s: when the bucket broke, the moon vanished from the sky
only its reflection went with the water.
Chiyono's verse ties the water and the moon together
where no water stays, no moon lives.
the story says Chiyono woke up on her first night at the temple
she comes to us as someone who practiced a long time first.

games.q: you're Chiyono, walking back with a full bucket and the moon in it. the bamboo hoop is cracking. what happens?
o: you tie it tighter and carry on.
the bottom falls out, and the moon in it is gone.
you set it down and fetch another bucket.
games.why: the hoop snaps, the water spills, the reflection disappears, and tradition says that is the moment she woke up.

practice: If there's a glass near you, pour a little into another cup or a sink and watch it go; if not, remember rain sliding off a roof, or a wave pulling back from the sand. Notice the moment the water leaves its shape.
Then let each out-breath spill the same way, holding nothing together.

wordCard.voice: No water. Chiyono's bucket breaks, the water spills, and the moon's reflection is gone, while the moon itself stays in the sky. Today's word.

orig.note: Japanese tsuki: moon. the one in Chiyono's bucket, and the one that stayed in the sky.

carryVoice: Your line: the bottom fell out. What spilled was only water, never the moon. Until tomorrow.
